source: built-in example (nma-inconsistency/index.html #src: 11 independent two-arm contrasts, treatments A-D), default options: fixed-effect model
plain: This analysis checked whether direct and indirect evidence agree in a network of 11 two-arm studies comparing 4 treatments, using a fixed-effect model. Direct and indirect evidence could be compared for 6 comparisons; for none of them did the two sources disagree by more than chance would readily explain (all P values at or above five per cent). The test of the network as a whole found no clear evidence of inconsistency (p = 0.979); this does not show that the network is consistent. Tests for inconsistency have low power, especially when comparisons rest on few studies, so they cannot rule inconsistency out. This summary describes agreement between sources of evidence; it does not show which treatment is better or whether any difference matters to patients.
methods: Each study contributed one contrast (the effect of one treatment relative to another, on the scale on which it was entered, with its standard error); only independent two-arm studies were accepted, and the network had to be connected. A network (consistency) model was fitted by weighted least squares with the basic parameters expressed against the first treatment in sorted label order, with weights equal to one over the sum of the squared standard error and the between-study variance τ². A fixed-effect model was used (τ² set to zero). Inconsistency was assessed by node-splitting (the approach of Dias and colleagues) for every comparison with direct evidence whose remaining studies still connect its two treatments: the direct estimate is the inverse-variance weighted mean of the studies of that comparison, and the indirect estimate is the same comparison estimated by the network model fitted to all other studies. The difference (direct minus indirect) has standard error √(SE²(direct) + SE²(indirect)) and was tested with a z statistic and a two-sided P value from the normal distribution. For independent two-arm studies this split is identical to the back-calculation method of netmeta (netsplit) at the same τ². A comparison labelled “A vs B” is the effect of A relative to B, with A and B in sorted label order; the app labels a comparison “inconsistent” when its P value is below five per cent. Global inconsistency was assessed with the design-by-treatment interaction test (the approach of Higgins and colleagues): the weighted sum of squares between the fitted values of the consistency model and of a model with one parameter for each design (each pair of treatments, as all studies have two arms), referred to a chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in the number of parameters. The plot shows 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± z × SE) for the direct and indirect estimates. No prediction intervals, treatment rankings or pooled network estimates are reported by this app. Analyses were run in allmeta nma-inconsistency <build.version> (commit <build.shortSha>).
results: The network included 11 two-arm studies of 4 treatments. The fixed-effect model was used. Node-splitting (6 comparisons; estimate with standard error, difference = direct minus indirect): A vs B: direct −0.302 (SE 0.051), indirect −0.285 (SE 0.099), difference −0.017 (SE 0.112), z = −0.15, p = 0.880; A vs C: direct −0.212 (SE 0.077), indirect −0.193 (SE 0.086), difference −0.018 (SE 0.115), z = −0.16, p = 0.873; B vs C: direct 0.092 (SE 0.084), indirect 0.098 (SE 0.084), difference −0.006 (SE 0.119), z = −0.05, p = 0.960; A vs D: direct −0.489 (SE 0.102), indirect −0.558 (SE 0.120), difference 0.068 (SE 0.158), z = 0.43, p = 0.665; B vs D: direct −0.250 (SE 0.180), indirect −0.212 (SE 0.094), difference −0.038 (SE 0.203), z = −0.19, p = 0.850; C vs D: direct −0.350 (SE 0.140), indirect −0.294 (SE 0.106), difference −0.056 (SE 0.176), z = −0.32, p = 0.750. No comparison had a P value below five per cent. The design-by-treatment interaction test gave Q = 0.19 (df = 3, p = 0.979).
flags: Tests for inconsistency have low power: a P value at or above five per cent is no clear evidence of inconsistency, not evidence of consistency.
Each comparison is tested separately; with several comparisons, some small P values are expected by chance alone.
The fixed-effect model ignores between-study heterogeneity, which can make inconsistency tests too liberal; the random-effects options estimate a shared τ² first.
